<reason>CON built the more coherent economic case (debt-to-GDP denominator dynamics, opportunity cost of foregone high-return investment, a concrete and non-evasive answer to the threshold pressure question) and then converted a key PRO concession into a decisive, unanswered rebuttal. When PRO admitted its rule was "a pause on addition, not a program of subtraction" [A2.4] with no quantifiable savings [A4.1], CON correctly identified that this contradicts the motion's actual demand for "deficit reduction" — a pause that doesn't shrink the certain interest cost PRO's whole case was built on is deficit maintenance, not reduction [B2.1, B4.2-B4.4, B5.1-B5.4]. PRO never directly rebutted this "zero reduction" critique in Rebuttal 2 or Closing, instead reasserting the certain-cost-vs-speculative-benefit asymmetry without showing its rule actually lowers the certain cost. PRO's honesty in refusing to invent a savings figure was commendable epistemic discipline, but it left the core mechanism of its case unresolved against CON's sharpest attack. CON also answered pressure questions more substantively (a real trigger condition, an explicit answer on tax cuts and targeted spending) while PRO's Q1 answer largely deflected. Both sides avoided fake citations and stayed within plausible background reasoning, but CON's case was more internally consistent by the end and left PRO's central claim structurally hollowed out.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's exploitation of PRO's concession that the rule is "a pause on addition, not subtraction" [A2.4/A4.1], turned into the closing argument that the rule produces zero actual deficit reduction while still sacrificing high-return investment [B4.2-B4.4, B5.1-B5.4] — a line of attack PRO never squarely answered.</best_rebuttal>
